chapter_theme: The impermanence of wealth (செல்வம் நிலையாமை): wealth wanes like the moon, sinks like a capsizing boat and is taken by the stronger, as honey is taken from bees; the lasting wealth is the Lord, and one who gives up his wealth and thinks of him need not fear Death.
structure_note: Most verses set fleeting wealth against the Lord as true wealth (168, 169, 173, 176); 171 and 175 share a closing line about being shown up and abandoned, and 172 and 174 urge giving wealth away.

168.reading: Before favour, king, elephants, chariots and wealth pass into others' hands, if with clear understanding, while life lasts, one joins the one who is true wealth, confusion ends; that is the great austerity.
168.nuance: செல்வன் (the wealthy one) is taken as the Lord, the wealth that is not lost. அருள் at the head of the list is odd among worldly goods; it may mean a patron's favour. Line 4 (மருளும் பினையவன்) is hard to construe.

169.reading: Wealth that bewilders is like the moving moon with its great waning, and needs no more said of it; seek the king of the gods without confusion, and he becomes great wealth, like a rain cloud.
169.nuance: The two images are paired: the moon that grows only to wane, and the rain cloud that pours. இரும்பிழப்பு is read as இரும் இழப்பு (great loss); வானவர் கோன் (king of the gods) is Siva here.

170.reading: Seeing that even their own shadow is no help to them, the foolish still sit saying 'this wealth is mine'; your life will go, though it was born together with the body; see the light the eye sees.
170.nuance: The shadow that cannot help its owner shows how little anything outside one is one's own. The last line (கண்ணது காணொளி) may mean simply 'see with your own eyes' or point to an inner light; both readings stand.

171.reading: Bees find the scent of flowers, gather the honey and its sweetness and store it on a branch; the strong drive them off and take it, and this is how what was gathered was shown up and abandoned.
171.nuance: The hoarder is the bee and the strong (வலியார்) are whoever takes the hoard: thieves, kings, heirs. The verse states the image and leaves the lesson to the reader.

172.reading: Be clear and settled, and once clear do not be troubled; do not churn about like a river in flood; turn your wealth away and get rid of it, and when Death comes you may even leap past him.
172.nuance: மாற்றிக் களைவீர் மறுத்து may mean giving the wealth away or renouncing it; either way the hold on it is broken. குதிக்கலும் ஆமே (one may even leap) echoes the old phrase for escaping Death; whether that means not dying, or meeting death unafraid and free, the verse doesn't say.

173.reading: The wealth and riches you delight in go like a boat on water that capsizes; people do not examine and see that a small casket has been set within the body that comes apart, as the means of release.
173.nuance: சிமிழ் (a small casket) is unexplained; it is traditionally taken as the place within the body where the Lord is found, such as the heart. The verse contrasts the boat that sinks with a treasure already inside.

174.reading: People say of their life, wife, children and brothers 'what limit is there to what is ours?'; to those who share out the bright wealth that comes to them, a helper who answers when called may come.
174.nuance: Line 2 (அளவு ஏது எமக்கு) may be boasting ('our wealth has no limit') or worry ('what is enough for us?'). கூவும் துணை (the helper who answers a call) may be the Lord or the merit of giving.

175.reading: Craving has grown great, and no one here holds to truth; there is one post to tie to and nine ways out; the mother and kin who set it up come and bow, and then, this is how they showed it up and abandoned it.
175.nuance: The post (தறி) is the body where the life is tethered, the nine ways its openings, as in 152. The last line repeats 171's, so the kin who raised the body leave it as the strong leave the bees' hive. Why the verse sits in a chapter on wealth is unclear unless the body is the first wealth.

176.reading: When the life leaves the body and runs, there is no way to fight it; think of the Lord, and Death's true messengers, who stand ready to release, will not even think of burning you.
176.nuance: அண்ணலை எண்ணும் can be a command ('think of the Lord') or describe those who do. The last two lines are hard to construe; the reading that Death's messengers spare the one who thinks of the Lord is the plainest but not certain.

links.note: Both use the honey bee whose stored honey others take. The Naladiyar spells out the lesson, that those who hoard without giving lose it all; Tirumular gives only the image.

Both tell the rich to give their wealth away in view of Death, but the Naladiyar says no one has ever leapt past Death and escaped, while Tirumular says one who sheds his wealth may leap past him. The conflict holds if Tirumular's leap means escaping death; if it means dying free of fear or bondage, the two agree.
Both use the phrase of leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்) as something attainable: the Kural through the power of austerity, Tirumular through letting go of wealth.
The two verses end with the same line (காட்டிக் கொடுத்தவர் கைவிட்ட வாறே): the bees' hoard taken by the strong, and the body left by the kin who raised it.
Both make wealth vanish without trace through a sudden image, the Naladiyar's lightning in a night cloud and Tirumular's capsizing boat; Tirumular adds a treasure in the body that does not sink.

168 urges joining the Lord who is true wealth while life lasts, before favour, kingdom and wealth go to others (பிறர்கொள்ளப் போவதன் முன்னம்). Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts (அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both turn the impermanence of wealth into a call for immediate action; Tirumular names the lasting thing as the Lord.

169 likens wealth to the moving moon that wanes greatly (இயக்குறு திங்கள் இரும்பிழப்பு ஒக்கும்). Naladiyar 125 likens the bond with the small to the full moon that wanes day by day (வைகலும் தேயுமே). The waning moon marks what is lost by its own nature, wealth in one and friendship in the other.

170 calls fools those who say 'this wealth is mine' (என்னது மாடென்று இருப்பர்கள் ஏழைகள்) though even their shadow does not help them. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 170 shows the 'mine' in action that the Kural tells one to cut.

171 has the bees gather honey and store it, only for the strong to drive them off and take it (அதுவலியார் கொள). Kural 1009 says wealth amassed without love, comfort or virtue is taken by others (ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்). The bee image of 171 is the Kural's maxim made a scene.

172 says give away your wealth and when Death comes you may even leap past him (கூற்றன் வருங்கால் குதிக்கலும் ஆமே). Naladiyar 5 says those who gave first will escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives (முன்னே கொடுத்தார் உயப்போவர்). Both promise escape from Death through giving, while Naladiyar 6, already linked, denies that anyone leapt Death.

172 opens: be clear and settled, once clear do not be troubled (தேற்றத் தெளிமின் தெளிந்தீர் கலங்கன்மின்). 1533 has the same call: be clear, become settled, then enter without wavering (தேறுமின் தேறித் தெளிமின் தெளிந்தபின் மாறுதல் இன்றி). The formula applies to wealth in 172 and to the six sects in 1533.

174 says a helper who answers when called may come to those who share out the bright wealth that comes to them (விரிவுசெய் வார்கட்குக் கூவும் துணையொன்று கூடலுமாமே). Kural 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make giving the way to gain support.

175 ends 'this is how those who showed it gave it up' (காட்டிக் கொடுத்தவர் கைவிட்ட வாறே), the line 171 also ends with. 2933, in the riddle chapter, ends with the same line after the fallen mango that calling the jackal cannot save. The near-repeat line closes three verses on things let go.

175 says there is one post to tie to and nine ways out (பூட்டுந் தறியொன்று போம்வழி ஒன்பது). 2025 has one herdsman with a staff and nine ways by which the senses come and go (போம்வழி ஒன்பது). The nine openings of the body are exits for the life in 175 and roads for the senses in 2025.

176 opens with the life leaving the body (உடம்போடு உயிரிடை விட்டோடும் போது), almost the Kural's words for the bond of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) in 338. The Kural ends on the bird gone; 176 adds that thinking of the Lord keeps Death's messengers from burning the life.

source_issues: 168 line 4 (மருளும் பினையவன்) and 176 lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
